13-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
14-declare_syntax_cat invAlt
15-syntax " | " caseArg " => " tacticSeq : invAlt
16-
17-/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
18-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/
19-declare_syntax_cat invAlts
20-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts
21-
22-/--
23-  `inversion h` behaves like `cases h` except that where `cases` would fail with
24-  > "Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation ...",
25-
26-  `inversion` instead leaves behind those unsolveable equations in the context.
27-  These equations arise from generalizing the indices of `h`'s type.
28-  In such cases, `h` itself is generalized with a heterogenenous equality `heq`
29-  to the corresponding constructor in each branch.
30-
31-  For instance, given a hypothesis `h : f n ≤ 0`,
32-  `inversion h` will produce one goal for the case `Nat.le.refl {n} : n ≤ n`
33-  with the equations `eq : f n = 0` and `heq : h ≍ Nat.le.refl`,
34-  rather than failing to solve `f n = 0`.
35-
36-  * If `inversion +clear h` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
37-    along with `h` if there are no dependencies on it.
38-    This is the usual behavior of `cases`.
39-  * The form `inversion t with (tac ...) | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...`
40-    is supported, similar to that of `cases` and `induction`.
41--/
42-syntax (name := inversion)
43-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (tacticSeq)? (colGe invAlts)*)? : tactic
44-
45-end Lean.Parser

49-/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
50-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
51-  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
52-  return decl.userName

54-/-- Get the string suffix of a name as a name -/
55-def _root_.Lean.Name.getSuffix : Name → Name
56-| .anonymous => .anonymous
57-| .str _ s => .str .anonymous s
58-| .num n _ => n.getSuffix

60-/--
61-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
62-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
63-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
64-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
65-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
66-
67-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
68-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
69-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
70-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
71-
72-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
73--/
74-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
75-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
76-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
77-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
78-  unless ms.size == 1 do
79-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
80-    else throwError m!"Failed"
81-  let mut mvs := ms
82-  let mut bis := bs
83-  let mut out : Expr := tp
84-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
85-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
86-    unless ms.size == 1 do
87-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
88-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
89-    bis := bis ++ bs
90-    out := tp
91-  return (mvs, bis, out)
92-
93-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
94-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
95-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
96-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
97-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
98-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
99-
100-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
101-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
102-  match eqs with
103-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
104-  | eq :: eqs =>
105-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
106-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
107-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
108-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
109-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
110-
111-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
112-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
113-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
114-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
115-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
116-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
117-    else return some { s with
118-      mvarId := mvarId,
119-      subst  := subst,
120-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
121-    }
122-
123-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
124-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
125-
126-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
127-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
128-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
129-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
130-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
131-    return { s with mvarId }
132-
133-end Lean.Meta

143-/--
144-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
145-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
146-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
147-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
148-  original `i`.
149-
150-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
151--/
152-elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
153-  let f ← elabTermForApply t
154-  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
155-    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
156-  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
157-  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
158-    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
159-      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
160-      catch _ => continue
161-  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
162-    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
163-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
164-  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)

166-structure InversionConfig where
167-  clear : Bool := false
168-
169-declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig

171-open Cases in
172-/-- Perform inversion on the given variable in the context of the given goal.
173-  Behaves like [Lean.Meta.Cases.cases] and generalizes indices if they aren't independent,
174-  except instead of calling [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs], which may fail
175-  if the generalizing equations can't all be destructed and substituted away,
176-  it calls our [unifyCasesEqs] above, which keeps unsolvable equations in the context. -/
177-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.inversion (mvarId : MVarId) (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig)
178-    (givenNames : Array AltVarNames := #[]) (interestingCtors? : Option (Array Name) := none) :
179-    TacticM (Array CasesSubgoal) := mvarId.withContext do
180-  let goal ← getMainGoal
181-  goal.withContext do
182-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
183-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
184-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
185-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
186-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
187-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
188-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
189-        else pure subgoals
190-      return subgoals
191-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
192-    else
193-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
194-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
195-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
196-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
197-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
198-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
199-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
200-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
201-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
202-        else pure subgoals
203-      return subgoals
204-
205-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
206-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
207-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
208-def evalInvAlt (goals : List MVarId) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
209-  match alt with
210-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
211-    if let some goal ← goals.findM? (matchTag tag.getId <$> ·.getUserName) then
212-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal]
213-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
214-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
215-    if !goals.isEmpty then
216-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics)
217-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
218-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
219-where
220-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
221-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
222-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
223-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
224-    unless goals.isEmpty do
225-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
226-    return goal
227-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
228-    let goalMsgs ← goals.mapM (.ofName <$> ·.getUserName)
229-    return if goals.isEmpty
230-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
231-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
232-
233-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
234-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
235-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$tactics?:tacticSeq]? $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
236-    let casesSubgoals ← (← getMainGoal).inversion (← getFVarId h) (← elabInversionConfig config)
237-    let mut goals ← casesSubgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
238-    if let some tactics := tactics?.join then
239-      let subgoals ← goals.mapM (evalTacticAt tactics)
240-      goals ← subgoals.flatten.filterM (not <$> ·.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned)
241-    if let some alts := alts? then
242-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
243-      for alt in expandedAlts do
244-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
245-        goals := goals.removeAll solvedGoals
246-      unless goals.isEmpty do
247-        reportUnsolvedGoals goals
248-    replaceMainGoal goals
249-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
250-where
251-  setUserName subgoal : TacticM MVarId := do
252-    if let some name := subgoal.ctorName then
253-      subgoal.mvarId.setUserName name.getSuffix
254-    return subgoal.mvarId
255-  expandInvAlts
256-    | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
257-      args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
258-    | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
259-
260-end Lean.Elab.Tactic

273-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
274-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
275-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
276-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
277-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
278-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
279-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
280-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
281-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
282-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/
283-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
284-  -- cases leq /- Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation 0 = f n -/
285-  inversion leq; assumption
286-
287-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
288-  inversion +clear leq; assumption
289-
290-/-- error: Unknown identifier `leq` -/

292-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
293-  inversion +clear leq
294-  guard_hyp leq
295-

297-  inversion leq with
298-  | refl heq eq =>
299-    guard_hyp heq : leq ≍ le.refl
300-    guard_hyp eq : 0 = f n
301-    assumption

14061397 --  The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
14071398 --  (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
14081399 --  number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a
14091400 --  terminating mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is
14101401 --  true.
1411---

14131404 --  by functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false`
14141405 --  in finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
14151406 --  argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether
14161407 --  a given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1417---

14201411 --  contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine

5151 --  For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar

6666 --  Compared to the Lean version above...
67---
67+
6868 --  - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions
6969 --    about the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the
7070 --    addition operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other
7575 --    formal definition, e.g., for implementing a compiler. The Lean
7676 --    version consistently omits all this information and concentrates on
7777 --    the abstract syntax only.
78---
78+
7979 --  - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its
8080 --    informality makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like
8181 --    discussions at the blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more
8282 --    important than nailing down every detail precisely.
83---
83+
8484 --    Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch
8585 --    freely among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of
8686 --    BNF they're using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready
8787 --    informal understanding is all that's important.
88---
88+
8989 --  It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones
9090 --  for communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
9191 --  implementations and proofs.

230224 --  The upshot of this section is that STLC types and terms are both
231225 --  written inside one pair of brackets, `<{ … }>`, and that `~e` inside
232226 --  the brackets escapes back to an arbitrary Lean expression:
233---
227+
234228 --  - `<{ Bool → Bool }>` is a type;
235---
229+
236230 --  - `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` is a term — a bare identifier inside the
237231 --    brackets is the object-language variable of that name, so `<{ x }>`
238232 --    is the variable `x`;
239---
233+
240234 --  - `<{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>` applies one Lean-level term to another.
241---
235+
242236 --  Lean works out from context which of the two a given bracket holds, so
243237 --  the same brackets serve for types, for terms, and — when we come to
244238 --  typing — for typing judgments too. How that works is in the collapsed
245239 --  blocks below; nothing later in the chapter depends on it.

507507 --  To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to consider.
508---
508+
509509 --  First, for the boolean part of the language, the situation is clear:
510510 --  `true` and `false` are the only values. An `if` expression is never a
511511 --  value.
512---
512+
513513 --  Second, an application is not a value: it represents a function being
514514 --  invoked on some argument, which clearly still has work left to do.
515---
515+
516516 --  Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
517---
517+
518518 --  - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is a value — i.e.,
519519 --    only if the function's body has been reduced (as much as it can be
520520 --    without knowing what argument it is going to be applied to).
521---
521+
522522 --  - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no matter whether `t`
523523 --    is one or not — in other words, we can say that reduction stops at
524524 --    abstractions.
525---
525+

527527 --  — for example,

556556 --  Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete* program.
557---
557+
558558 --  Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any undefined
559559 --  variables. We'll see shortly how to define the *free* variables in a
560560 --  STLC term. A complete program, then, is one that is *closed* — that is,
561561 --  that contains no free variables.
562---
562+
563563 --  (Conversely, a term that may contain free variables is often called an
564564 --  *open term*.)
565---
565+

567567 --  to worry about whether variables are values, since we'll always be
568568 --  reducing programs "from the outside in," and that means the `step`
575575 --  to define the operational semantics of function application, where we
576576 --  will need to substitute the argument term for the function parameter in
577577 --  the function's body. For example, we reduce

10611045 --  Consider checking that `λx:T₁₁. t₁₂` has type `T₁₁ → T₁₂`. Intuitively,
10621046 --  we need to check that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`. However, we have removed
10631047 --  the binder `λx`, so `x` may occur free in `t₁₂` (that is, `t₁₂` may be
10661050 --  of `x`. Similarly, `t₁₂` itself could contain abstractions, and
10671051 --  typechecking their bodies could require looking up the declared types
10681052 --  of yet more free variables.
1069---

10721056 --  occur free in a term — that is, Γ is a partial map from variables to
10731057 --  types.

6---  # StlcProp: Properties of STLC
7-
8---  In this chapter, we develop the fundamental theory of the Simply Typed
9---  Lambda Calculus — in particular, the type safety theorem.
10---
11---  We pick up where the Stlc chapter left off, so everything below lives
12---  in the same namespace as the definitions it is about.

18---  ## Canonical Forms
19-
20---  As we saw for the very simple language in the Types chapter, the first
21---  step in establishing basic properties of reduction and types is to
22---  identify the possible *canonical forms* (i.e., well-typed values)
23---  belonging to each type. For `Bool`, these are again the boolean values
24---  `true` and `false`; for arrow types, they are lambda-abstractions.
25-
26---  Formally, we will need these lemmas only for terms that are not only
27---  well typed but *closed* — i.e., well typed in the empty context.
28-
29-theorem canonical_forms_bool (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : t.IsValue) :
30-    t = <{ true }> ∨ t = <{ false }> := by
31-  cases hv with
32-  | abs x T t₁ => cases hT
33-  | tru => left; rfl
34-  | fls => right; rfl
35-
36-theorem canonical_forms_fun (t : Tm) (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
37-    (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T₁ → ~T₂ }>) (hv : t.IsValue) :
38-    ∃ x u, t = <{ λ ~x : ~T₁ . ~u }> := by
39-  cases hv with
40-  | abs x T t₁ => cases hT with | abs _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
41-    exists x, t₁
42-  | tru => cases hT
43-  | fls => cases hT

45---  ## Progress
46-
47---  The *progress* theorem tells us that closed, well-typed terms are not
48---  stuck: either a well-typed term is a value, or it can take a reduction
49---  step. The proof is a relatively straightforward extension of the
50---  progress proof we saw in the Types chapter. We give the proof in
51---  English first, then the formal version.
52-
53---  *Proof*: By induction on the derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
54---
55---  - The last rule of the derivation cannot be `HasType.var`, since a
56---    variable is never well typed in an empty context.
57---
58---  - The `HasType.tru`, `HasType.fls`, and `HasType.abs` cases are
59---    trivial, since in each of these cases we can see by inspecting the
60---    rule that `t` is a value.
61---
62---  - If the last rule of the derivation is `HasType.app`, then `t` has the
63---    form `t₁ t₂` for some `t₁` and `t₂`, where `⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T` and
64---    `⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂` for some type `T₂`. The induction hypothesis for the
65---    first subderivation says that either `t₁` is a value or else it can
66---    take a reduction step.
67---
68---    - If `t₁` is a value, then consider `t₂`, which by the induction
69---      hypothesis for the second subderivation must also either be a value
70---      or take a step.
71---
72---      - Suppose `t₂` is a value. Since `t₁` is a value with an arrow
73---        type, it must be a lambda abstraction; hence `t₁ t₂` can take a
74---        step by `Step.appAbs`.
75---
76---      - Otherwise, `t₂` can take a step, and hence so can `t₁ t₂` by
77---        `Step.app2`.
78---
79---    - If `t₁` can take a step, then so can `t₁ t₂` by `Step.app1`.
80---
81---  - If the last rule of the derivation is `HasType.ite`, then
82---    `t = if t₁ then t₂ else t₃`, where `t₁` has type `Bool`. The first IH
83---    says that `t₁` either is a value or takes a step.
84---
85---    - If `t₁` is a value, then since it has type `Bool` it must be either
86---      `true` or `false`. If it is `true`, then `t` steps to `t₂`;
87---      otherwise it steps to `t₃`.
88---
89---    - Otherwise, `t₁` takes a step, and therefore so does `t` (by
90---      `Step.ifStep`).
91-
92-theorem progress (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) :
93-    t.IsValue ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
94-  generalize hΓ : (∅ : Context) = Γ at hT
95-  induction hT with
96-  | var Γ x T₁ h =>
97-    subst hΓ
98-    -- Contradictory: variables cannot be typed in an empty context.
99-    rw [PartialMap.getElem_empty] at h
100-    cases h
101-  | abs => left; constructor
102-  | tru => left; constructor
103-  | fls => left; constructor
104-  | app Γ T₁ T₂ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
105-    -- `t = t₁ t₂`.  Proceed by cases on whether `t₁` is a value or steps.
106-    right
107-    cases ih₁ hΓ with
108-    | inl hv₁ =>
109-      cases ih₂ hΓ with
110-      | inl hv₂ =>
111-        obtain ⟨x, u, rfl⟩ := canonical_forms_fun t₁ _ _ (hΓ ▸ h₁) hv₁
112-        exists <{ [~x := ~t₂] ~u }>
113-        constructor
114-        assumption
115-      | inr hs₂ =>
116-        obtain ⟨t₂', h⟩ := hs₂
117-        exists <{ ~t₁ ~t₂' }>
118-        constructor <;> assumption
119-    | inr hs₁ =>
120-      obtain ⟨t₁', h⟩ := hs₁
121-      exists <{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>
122-      constructor <;> assumption
123-  | ite Γ t₁ t₂ t₃ T₁ h₁ h₂ h₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
124-    right
125-    cases ih₁ hΓ with
126-    | inl hv₁ =>
127-      cases canonical_forms_bool t₁ (hΓ ▸ h₁) hv₁ with
128-      | inl he =>
129-        subst he
130-        exists t₂
131-        constructor
132-      | inr he =>
133-        subst he
134-        exists t₃
135-        constructor
136-    | inr hs₁ =>
137-      obtain ⟨t₁', h⟩ := hs₁
138-      exists <{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
139-      constructor
140-      assumption

152---  ## Preservation
153-
154---  The other half of the type soundness property is the preservation of
155---  types during reduction. For this part, we'll need to develop some
156---  technical machinery for reasoning about variables and substitution.
157---  Working from top to bottom (from the high-level property we are
158---  actually interested in to the lowest-level technical lemmas that are
159---  needed by various cases of the more interesting proofs), the story goes
160---  like this:
161---
162---  - The *preservation theorem* is proved by induction on a typing
163---    derivation and case analysis on the step relation, pretty much as we
164---    did in the Types chapter. The one case that is significantly
165---    different is the one for the `Step.appAbs` rule, whose definition
166---    uses the substitution operation. To see that this step preserves
167---    typing, we need to know that the substitution itself does. So we
168---    prove a...
169---
170---  - *substitution lemma*, stating that substituting a (closed,
171---    well-typed) term `s` for a variable `x` in a term `t` preserves the
172---    type of `t`. The proof goes by induction on the form of `t` and
173---    requires looking at all the different cases in the definition of
174---    substitution. This time, for the variables case, we discover that we
175---    need to deduce from the fact that a term `s` has type S in the empty
176---    context the fact that `s` has type S in every context. For this we
177---    prove a...
178---
179---  - *weakening* lemma, showing that typing is preserved under
180---    "extensions" to the context `Γ`.
181---
182---  To make Lean happy, though, we need to formalize the story in the
183---  opposite order, starting with weakening...
184-
185---  ### The Weakening Lemma
186-
187---  First, we show that typing is preserved under "extensions" to the
188---  context `Γ`. (Recall map inclusion, `Γ ⊆ Γ'`, from the `Typeclasses`
189---  chapter.)
190-
191--- IN PROGRESS
192-theorem weakening (Γ Γ' : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty)
193-    (hi : Γ ⊆ Γ') (hT : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) : <{ ~Γ' ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
194-  induction hT generalizing Γ' with
195-  | var _ x _ h => exact .var _ x _ (hi h)
196-  | abs _ x _ _ _ _ ih => exact .abs _ x _ _ _ (ih _ (PartialMap.update_subset _ _ _ _ hi))
197-  | app _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hi) (ih₂ _ hi)
198-  | tru => exact .tru _
199-  | fls => exact .fls _
200-  | ite _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ => exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hi) (ih₂ _ hi) (ih₃ _ hi)
201-
202---  The following simple corollary is what we actually need below.
203-
204-theorem weakening_empty (Γ : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) :
205-    <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> :=
206-  weakening _ _ _ _
207-    (fun h => by
208-      rw [PartialMap.getElem_empty] at h
209-      cases h) hT
210-
211---  ### The Substitution Lemma
212-
213---  Now we come to the conceptual heart of the proof that reduction
214---  preserves types — namely, the observation that *substitution* preserves
215---  types.
216-
217---  Formally, the so-called *substitution lemma* says this: Suppose we have
218---  a term `t` with a free variable `x`, and suppose we've assigned a type
219---  `T` to `t` under the assumption that `x` has some type `U`. Also,
220---  suppose that we have some other term `v` and that we've shown that `v`
221---  has type `U`. Then, since `v` satisfies the assumption we made about
222---  `x` when typing `t`, we can substitute `v` for each of the occurrences
223---  of `x` in `t` and obtain a new term that still has type `T`.
224-
225--- IN PROGRESS
226-theorem substitution_preserves_typing (Γ : Context) (x : String) (U : Ty)
227-    (t v : Tm) (T : Ty)
228-    (hT : <{ ~x ↦ ~U ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hv : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~v ⦂ ~U }>) :
229-    <{ ~Γ ⊢ [~x := ~v] ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
230-  -- By induction on `t`; in each case we get at the derivation of `hT`.
231-  induction t generalizing Γ T with
232-  | var y =>
233-    cases hT with
234-    | var _ _ _ h =>
235-      by_cases hxy : x = y
236-      · subst hxy
237-        rw [PartialMap.update_eq] at h
238-        rw [subst_var_eq]
239-        have hUT : U = T := Option.some.inj h
240-        subst hUT
241-        exact weakening_empty _ _ _ hv
242-      · rw [PartialMap.update_neq hxy] at h
243-        rw [subst_var_ne _ _ _ hxy]
244-        exact .var _ y _ h
245-  | app t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
246-    cases hT with
247-    | app _ _ _ _ _ h₁ h₂ => rw [subst_app]; exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ _ h₁) (ih₂ _ _ h₂)
248-  | abs y S t₁ ih =>
249-    cases hT with
250-    | abs _ _ _ _ _ h =>
251-      by_cases hxy : x = y
252-      · subst hxy
253-        rw [subst_abs_eq]
254-        rw [PartialMap.update_shadow] at h
255-        exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ h
256-      · rw [subst_abs_ne _ _ _ _ _ hxy]
257-        rw [PartialMap.update_permute (Ne.symm hxy)] at h
258-        exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ (ih _ _ h)
259-  | tru => cases hT with | tru => rw [subst_tru]; exact .tru _
260-  | fls => cases hT with | fls => rw [subst_fls]; exact .fls _
261-  | ite c t e ihc iht ihe =>
262-    cases hT with
263-    | ite _ _ _ _ _ h₁ h₂ h₃ =>
264-      rw [subst_ite]
265-      exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ihc _ _ h₁) (iht _ _ h₂) (ihe _ _ h₃)
266-
267---  The substitution lemma can be viewed as a kind of "commutation
268---  property." Intuitively, it says that substitution and typing can be
269---  done in either order: we can either assign types to the terms `t` and
270---  `v` separately (under suitable contexts) and then combine them using
271---  substitution, or we can substitute first and then assign a type to
272---  `[x:=v] t`; the result is the same either way.
273---
274---  *Proof*: We show, by induction on `t`, that for all `T` and `Γ`, if
275---  `x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` and `⊢ v ⦂ U`, then `Γ ⊢ [x:=v]t ⦂ T`.
276---
277---  - If `t` is a variable there are two cases to consider, depending on
278---    whether `t` is `x` or some other variable.
279---
280---    - If `t = x`, then from the fact that `x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ x ⦂ T` we conclude
281---      that `U = T`. We must show that `[x:=v]x = v` has type `T` under
282---      `Γ`, given the assumption that `v` has type `U = T` under the empty
283---      context. This follows from the weakening lemma.
284---
285---    - If `t` is some variable `y` that is not equal to `x`, then we need
286---      only note that `y` has the same type under `x ↦ U; Γ` as under `Γ`.
287---
288---  - If `t` is an abstraction `λy:S. t₀`, then `T = S→T₁` and the IH tells
289---    us, for all `Γ'` and `T₀`, that if `x ↦ U; Γ' ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₀`, then
290---    `Γ' ⊢ [x:=v]t₀ ⦂ T₀`. Moreover, by inspecting the typing rules we see
291---    it must be the case that `y ↦ S; x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`.
292---
293---    The substitution in the conclusion behaves differently depending on
294---    whether `x` and `y` are the same variable.
295---
296---    First, suppose `x = y`. Then, by the definition of substitution,
297---    `[x:=v]t = t`, so we just need to show `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`. Using
298---    `HasType.abs`, we need to show that `y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`. But we know
299---    `y ↦ S; x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`, and the claim follows since `x = y`.
300---
301---    Second, suppose `x <> y`. Again, using `HasType.abs`, we need to show
302---    that `y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ [x:=v]t₀ ⦂ T₁`. Since `x <> y`, we have
303---    `y ↦ S; x ↦ U; Γ = x ↦ U; y ↦ S; Γ`. So we have
304---    `x ↦ U; y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`. Then, the the IH applies (taking
305---    `Γ' = y ↦ S; Γ`), giving us `y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ [x:=v]t₀ ⦂ T₁`, as required.
306---
307---  - If `t` is an application `t₁ t₂`, the result follows
308---    straightforwardly from the definition of substitution and the
309---    induction hypotheses.
310---
311---  - The remaining cases are similar to the application case.
312-
313---  One technical subtlety in the statement of the above lemma is that we
314---  assume `v` has type `U` in the *empty* context — in other words, we
315---  assume `v` is closed. (Since we are using a simple definition of
316---  substitution that is not capture-avoiding, it doesn't make sense to
317---  substitute non-closed terms into other terms. Fortunately, closed terms
318---  are all we need!)
319-

324-
325--- IN PROGRESS
326-theorem substitution_preserves_typing_from_typing_ind (Γ : Context) (x : String) (U : Ty)
327-    (t v : Tm) (T : Ty)
328-    (hT : <{ ~x ↦ ~U ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hv : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~v ⦂ ~U }>) :
329-    <{ ~Γ ⊢ [~x := ~v] ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by

332---  ### Main Theorem
333-
334---  We now have the ingredients we need to prove preservation: if a closed,
335---  well-typed term `t` has type `T` and takes a step to `t'`, then `t'` is
336---  also a closed term with type `T`. In other words, the small-step
337---  reduction relation preserves types.
338-
339--- IN PROGRESS
340-theorem preservation (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty)
341-    (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hs : t ⟶ t') : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t' ⦂ ~T }> := by
342-  generalize hΓ : (∅ : Context) = Γ at hT
343-  induction hT generalizing t' with
344-  | var => cases hs
345-  | abs => cases hs
346-  | tru => cases hs
347-  | fls => cases hs
348-  | app Γ T₁ T₂ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
349-    subst hΓ
350-    cases hs with
351-    | appAbs _ _ _ _ _ =>
352-      -- The one interesting case: the desired result is the substitution lemma.
353-      cases h₁ with
354-      | abs _ _ _ _ _ hb => exact substitution_preserves_typing _ _ _ _ _ _ hb h₂
355-    | app1 _ t₁' _ h => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ t₁' h rfl) h₂
356-    | app2 _ _ t₂' _ h => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ h₁ (ih₂ t₂' h rfl)
357-  | ite Γ t₁ t₂ t₃ T₁ h₁ h₂ h₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
358-    subst hΓ
359-    cases hs with
360-    | ifTrue => exact h₂
361-    | ifFalse => exact h₃
362-    | ifStep _ t₁' _ _ h => exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ t₁' h rfl) h₂ h₃
363-
364---  *Proof*: By induction on the derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
365---
366---  - We can immediately rule out `HasType.var`, `HasType.abs`,
367---    `HasType.tru`, and `HasType.fls` as final rules in the derivation,
368---    since in each of these cases `t` cannot take a step.
369---
370---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `HasType.app`, then
371---    `t = t₁ t₂`, and there are subderivations showing that `⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂→T`
372---    and `⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂` plus two induction hypotheses: (1) `t₁ ⟶ t₁'` implies
373---    `⊢ t₁' ⦂ T₂→T` and (2) `t₂ ⟶ t₂'` implies `⊢ t₂' ⦂ T₂`. There are now
374---    three subcases to consider, one for each rule that could be used to
375---    show that `t₁ t₂` takes a step to `t'`.
376---
377---    - If `t₁ t₂` takes a step by `Step.app1`, with `t₁` stepping to
378---      `t₁'`, then, by the first IH, `t₁'` has the same type as `t₁`
379---      (`⊢ t₁' ⦂ T₂→T`), and hence by `HasType.app` `t₁' t₂` has type `T`.
380---
381---    - The `Step.app2` case is similar, using the second IH.
382---
383---    - If `t₁ t₂` takes a step by `Step.appAbs`, then `t₁ = λx:T₀. t₀` and
384---      `t₁ t₂` steps to `[x0:=t₂]t₀`; the desired result now follows from
385---      the substitution lemma.
386---
387---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `HasType.ite`, then
388---    `t = if t₁ then t₂ else t₃`, with `⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₁`, and
389---    `⊢ t₃ ⦂ T₁`, and with three induction hypotheses: (1) `t₁ ⟶ t₁'`
390---    implies `⊢ t₁' ⦂ Bool`, (2) `t₂ ⟶ t₂'` implies `⊢ t₂' ⦂ T₁`, and (3)
391---    `t₃ ⟶ t₃'` implies `⊢ t₃' ⦂ T₁`.
392---
393---    There are again three subcases to consider, depending on how `t`
394---    steps.
395---
396---    - If `t` steps to `t₂` or `t₃` by `Step.ifTrue` or `Step.ifFalse`,
397---      the result is immediate, since `t₂` and `t₃` have the same type as
398---      `t`.
399---
400---    - Otherwise, `t` steps by `Step.ifStep`, and the desired conclusion
401---      follows directly from the first induction hypothesis.
402-

434-
435---  Another nice property of the STLC is that types are unique: a given
436---  term (in a given context) has at most one type.
437-
438--- AI
439-theorem unique_types (Γ : Context) (e : Tm) (T T' : Ty)

443---  ## Context Invariance (Optional)
444-
445---  Another standard technical lemma associated with typed languages is
446---  *context invariance*. It states that typing is preserved under
447---  "inessential changes" to the context `Γ` — in particular, changes that
448---  do not affect any of the free variables of the term. In this section,
449---  we establish this property for our system, introducing some other
450---  standard terminology on the way.
451---
452---  First, we need to define the *free variables* in a term — i.e.,
453---  variables that are used in the term in positions that are *not* in the
454---  scope of an enclosing function abstraction binding a variable of the
455---  same name.
456---
457---  More technically, a variable `x` *appears free in* a term *t* if `t`
458---  contains some occurrence of `x` that is not under an abstraction
459---  labeled `x`. For example:
460---
461---  - `y` appears free, but `x` does not, in `λx:T→U. x y`
462---  - both `x` and `y` appear free in `(λx:T→U. x y) x`
463---  - no variables appear free in `λx:T→U. λy:T. x y`
464---

473-  | var : x ∈ᶠ (Tm.var x)
474-  | app1 (t₁ t₂ : Tm) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₁) : x ∈ᶠ <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>
475-  | app2 (t₁ t₂ : Tm) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₂) : x ∈ᶠ <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>

485---  The *free variables* of a term are just the variables that appear free
486---  in it. This gives us another way to define *closed* terms — arguably a
487---  better one, since it applies even to ill-typed terms. Indeed, this is
488---  the standard definition of the term "closed."

490-def Tm.Closed (t : Tm) : Prop := ∀ x, ¬ x ∈ᶠ t

492---  Conversely, an *open* term is one that may contain free variables.
493---  (I.e., every term is an open term; the closed terms are a subset of the
494---  open ones. "Open" precisely means "possibly containing free
495---  variables.")

497---  ### Exercise (1 star): afi ⭐
498-

503---  rule.) Although this is a rather low-level, technical definition,
504---  understanding it is crucial to understanding substitution and its

507---  Next, we show that if a variable `x` appears free in a term `t`, and if
508---  we know `t` is well typed in context `Γ`, then it must be the case that
509---  `Γ` assigns a type to `x`.
510-
511--- IN PROGRESS
512-theorem free_in_context (x : String) (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (Γ : Context)
513-    (ha : x ∈ᶠ t) (hT : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) : ∃ T', Γ[x] = some T' := by
514-  sorry
515-
516---  *Proof*: We show, by induction on the proof that `x` appears free in
517---  `t`, that, for all contexts `Γ`, if `t` is well typed under `Γ`, then
518---  `Γ` assigns some type to `x`.
519---
520---  - If the last rule used is `AppearsFreeIn.var`, then `t = x`, and from
521---    the assumption that `t` is well typed under `Γ` we have immediately
522---    that `Γ` assigns a type to `x`.
523---
524---  - If the last rule used is `AppearsFreeIn.app1`, then `t = t₁ t₂` and
525---    `x` appears free in `t₁`. Since `t` is well typed under `Γ`, we can
526---    see from the typing rules that `t₁` must also be, and the IH then
527---    tells us that `Γ` assigns `x` a type.
528---
529---  - Almost all the other cases are similar: `x` appears free in a subterm
530---    of `t`, and since `t` is well typed under `Γ`, we know the subterm of
531---    `t` in which `x` appears is well typed under `Γ` as well, and the IH
532---    gives us exactly the conclusion we want.
533---
534---  - The only remaining case is `AppearsFreeIn.abs`. In this case
535---    `t = λy:T₁. t₁` and `x` appears free in `t₁`, and we also know that
536---    `x` is different from `y`. The difference from the previous cases is
537---    that, whereas `t` is well typed under `Γ`, its body `t₁` is well
538---    typed under `y ↦ T₁; Γ`, so the IH allows us to conclude that `x` is
539---    assigned some type by the extended context `y ↦ T₁; Γ`. To conclude
540---    that `Γ` assigns a type to `x`, we appeal to lemma
541---    `PartialMap.update_neq`, noting that `x` and `y` are different
542---    variables.

557---  Finally, we establish *context invariance*. It is useful in cases when
558---  we have a proof of some typing relation `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`, and we need to
559---  replace `Γ` by a different context `Γ'`. When is it safe to do this?
560---  Intuitively, it must at least be the case that `Γ'` assigns the same
561---  types as `Γ` to all the variables that appear free in `t`. In fact,
562---  this is the only condition that is needed.
563-
564--- IN PROGRESS
565-theorem context_invariance (Γ Γ' : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty)
566-    (hT : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hf : ∀ x, x ∈ᶠ t → Γ[x] = Γ'[x]) :
567-    <{ ~Γ' ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
568-  sorry
569-
570---  *Proof*: By induction on the derivation of `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`.
571---
572---  - If the last rule in the derivation was `HasType.var`, then `t = x`
573---    and `Γ x = T`. By assumption, `Γ' x = T` as well, and hence
574---    `Γ' ⊢ t ⦂ T` by `HasType.var`.
575---
576---  - If the last rule was `HasType.abs`, then `t = λy:T₂. t₁`, with
577---    `T = T₂ → T₁` and `y ↦ T₂; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁`. The induction hypothesis
578---    states that for any context `Γ''`, if `y ↦ T₂; Γ` and `Γ''` assign
579---    the same types to all the free variables in `t₁`, then `t₁` has type
580---    `T₁` under `Γ''`. Let `Γ'` be a context which agrees with `Γ` on the
581---    free variables in `t`; we must show `Γ' ⊢ λy:T₂. t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁`.
582---
583---    By `HasType.abs`, it suffices to show that `y ↦ T₂; Γ' ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁`. By
584---    the IH (setting `Γ'' = y ↦ T₂;Γ'`), it suffices to show that
585---    `y ↦ T₂;Γ` and `y ↦ T₂;Γ'` agree on all the variables that appear
586---    free in `t₁`.
587---
588---    Any variable occurring free in `t₁` must be either `y` or some other
589---    variable. `y ↦ T₂; Γ` and `y ↦ T₂; Γ'` clearly agree on `y`.
590---    Otherwise, note that any variable other than `y` that occurs free in
591---    `t₁` also occurs free in `t = λy:T₂. t₁`, and by assumption `Γ` and
592---    `Γ'` agree on all such variables; hence so do `y ↦ T₂; Γ` and
593---    `y ↦ T₂; Γ'`.
594---
595---  - If the last rule was `HasType.app`, then `t = t₁ t₂`, with
596---    `Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T` and `Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂`. One induction hypothesis states
597---    that for all contexts `Γ'`, if `Γ'` agrees with `Γ` on the free
598---    variables in `t₁`, then `t₁` has type `T₂ → T` under `Γ'`; there is a
599---    similar IH for `t₂`. We must show that `t₁ t₂` also has type `T`
600---    under `Γ'`, given the assumption that `Γ'` agrees with `Γ` on all the
601---    free variables in `t₁ t₂`. By `HasType.app`, it suffices to show that
602---    `t₁` and `t₂` each have the same type under `Γ'` as under `Γ`. But
603---    all free variables in `t₁` are also free in `t₁ t₂`, and similarly
604---    for `t₂`; hence the desired result follows from the induction
605---    hypotheses.
606-

763---  ### Exercise: STLC with Arithmetic
764-
765---  To see how the STLC might function as the core of a real programming
766---  language, let's extend it with a concrete base type of numbers and some
767---  constants and primitive operators.
768---
769---  The arithmetic we are adding is the arithmetic of the Slang chapter —
770---  numeric constants and multiplication — together with the successor,
771---  predecessor, and zero-test operations of the Types chapter. What is new
772---  is the setting: those operations now live in a language that also has
773---  variables, abstraction, and application, so an arithmetic computation
774---  can be packaged up as a function and passed around as a value.
775-
776-namespace StlcArith
777-
778-open scoped MyGetElem
779-
780---  To types, we add a base type of natural numbers (and remove booleans,
781---  for brevity).
782-
783-inductive Ty where
784-  | arrow (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
785-  | nat
786-
787---  To terms, we add natural number constants, along with successor,
788---  predecessor, multiplication, and zero-testing.
789-
790-inductive Tm where
791-  | var (x : String)
792-  | app (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
793-  | abs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t : Tm)
794-  | const (n : Nat)
795-  | succ (t : Tm)
796-  | pred (t : Tm)
797-  | mult (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
798-  | ite0 (c t e : Tm)
799-
800---  `StlcArith` is a **different** language from the STLC of this chapter,
801---  not an extension of it, so it needs its own concrete syntax. Rather
802---  than invent a new one, we reuse the grammars set up in the Stlc chapter
803---  — the syntax categories `stlcTy`, `stlcTm`, and `stlcVar` — and give
804---  them a new meaning here. Terms and types of this language are therefore
805---  written inside the same `<{ … }>` brackets, with the same `~e` escape
806---  back to Lean.
807-
808---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: types)
809---  The type grammar needs no new productions: `Nat` is a bare identifier,
810---  which the template already accepts, and arrows and parentheses are
811---  unchanged. Only the `macro_rules` are new, and they differ from the
812---  STLC's in just two places — the identifier `Nat` names this language's
813---  base type, and the arrow builds this language's `StlcArith.Ty.arrow`.
814-
815-scoped macro_rules (kind := Stlc.tyBracket)
816-  | `(<{ ~$T:term }>)    => pure T
817-  | `(<{ ($T:stlcTy) }>) => `(<{ $T:stlcTy }>)
818-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
819-      match x.getId.toString with
820-      | "Nat" => `(Ty.nat)
821-      | _ => `(($x : Ty))
822-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy → $T₂:stlcTy }>)  => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
823-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy -> $T₂:stlcTy }>) => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
824---  END DETAILS
825-
826---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: terms)
827---  Terms do need new productions: a numeral, an infix `*`, and the zero
828---  test. Multiplication binds looser than application and tighter than
829---  `λ`, so `x * y z` multiplies `x` by the application `y z`; it
830---  associates to the right, so `x * y * z` is `x * (y * z)`.
831---
832---  `succ` and `pred` get no production of their own. Making them keywords
833---  would reserve those words globally — and we would then be unable to
834---  write `succ` as a case name in a proof, including for Lean's own `Nat`.
835---  Instead they are written as though they were functions applied to an
836---  argument, `succ t`, and the application rule below recognizes them.
837---  `if0` **is** a keyword, since `then` and `else` leave no other option;
838---  that is why the constructor above is called `StlcArith.Tm.ite0` rather
839---  than `if0`, just as the STLC's conditional is `Stlc.Tm.ite`.
840-
841-scoped syntax:max num : stlcTm
842-scoped syntax:60 stlcTm:61 " * " stlcTm:60 : stlcTm
843-scoped syntax:50 "if0 " stlcTm:51 " then " stlcTm:50 " else " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
844-
845-open Lean in
846-scoped macro_rules (kind := Stlc.tmBracket)
847-  | `(<{ ~$e:term }>)    => pure e
848-  | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)
849-  | `(<{ $n:num }>)      => `(Tm.const $n)
850-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
851-      match x.getId.toString with
852-      | "Nat"  => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`Nat` is a type, not a term"
853-      | "succ" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`succ` must be applied to an argument"
854-      | "pred" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`pred` must be applied to an argument"
855-      | _      => `(Tm.var $(quote x.getId.toString))
856-  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm $t₂:stlcTm }>) =>
857-      match t₁ with
858-      | `(stlcTm| $f:ident) =>
859-          match f.getId.toString with
860-          | "succ" => `(Tm.succ <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
861-          | "pred" => `(Tm.pred <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
862-          | _      => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
863-      | _ => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
864-  | `(<{ λ $x : $T . $t }>) => do
865-      `(Tm.abs $(← Stlc.varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
866-  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm * $t₂:stlcTm }>) => `(Tm.mult <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
867-  | `(<{ if0 $c then $t else $e }>) =>
868-      `(Tm.ite0 <{ $c:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $e:stlcTm }>)
869---  END DETAILS
870-
871---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing it back)
872---  As in the Stlc chapter, a delaborator runs the grammar backwards, so
873---  that goals mentioning these terms and types read in the concrete
874---  syntax. The parenthesizers registered there are for the whole syntax
875---  category, so they serve this language too and are not repeated.

877-open Lean in
878-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare variable in `stlcTm` rather than as reserved syntax? -/
879-def isPlainTmVarName (s : String) : Bool :=
880-  Stlc.isPlainName s && s != "Nat" && s != "succ" && s != "pred"
881-
882-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
883-/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
884-partial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
885-  let stx ←
886-    match_expr ← getExpr with
887-    | Ty.nat => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Nat):ident)
888-    | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
889-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
890-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
891-        `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
892-    | _ => do
893-        match ← delab with
894-        | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
895-        | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
896-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
897-
898-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
899-/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
900-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
901-  let stx ←
902-    match_expr ← getExpr with
903-    | Tm.var _ => do
904-        let x ← withAppArg delab
905-        match x with
906-        | `($s:str) =>
907-            if isPlainTmVarName s.getString then
908-              `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
909-            else
910-              let var : Term := mkIdent ``StlcArith.Tm.var
911-              `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
912-        | _ =>
913-            let var : Term := mkIdent ``StlcArith.Tm.var
914-            `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
915-    | Tm.const _ => do
916-        let n ← withAppArg delab
917-        match n with
918-        | `($n:num) => `(stlcTm| $n:num)
919-        | _ =>
920-            let const : Term := mkIdent ``StlcArith.Tm.const
921-            `(stlcTm| ~($const $n))
922-    | Tm.app _ _ => do
923-        let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
924-        let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner
925-        `(stlcTm| $f $a)
926-    | Tm.abs _ _ _ => do
927-        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg Stlc.delabVarInner
928-        let T ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
929-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
930-        `(stlcTm| λ $x : $T . $t)
931-    | Tm.succ _ => do
932-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
933-        `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `succ):ident $t)
934-    | Tm.pred _ => do
935-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
936-        `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `pred):ident $t)
937-    | Tm.mult _ _ => do
938-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner

654642 --  *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T`, then either `t` is a value or else `t ⟶ t'`
655643 --  for some `t'`.
656---
644+
657645 --  *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
658---
646+
659647 --  - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
660648 --    `t = if t1 then t2
661649 --        else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
662650 --    `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
663651 --    to some `t1'`.
664---
652+
665653 --    - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemmas and the fact
666654 --      that `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that `t1` is a boolean value
667655 --      (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e., it is either `true` or `false`. If
668656 --      `t1 = true`, then `t` steps to `t2` by `ifTrue`, while if
669657 --      `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`. Either way, `t`
670658 --      can step, which is what we wanted to show.
